lessonTitle: Full Blood Count, Coagulation and Transfusion

blocks.text: A 54-year-old woman is listed for routine knee surgery. Her pre-operative blood count reads haemoglobin 92 g/L with a mean cell volume of 71 fL. Nobody has asked about her stools. A single number on a printout has just changed the question from whether she can have an operation to why she is anaemic, and the blood film and ferritin will decide what happens next.

blocks.markdown: **A full blood count (FBC) is a machine-counted profile of the red cells, white cells and platelets in a venous EDTA sample.** The first step is to ask which line is abnormal, then classify. Typical adult reference ranges differ between laboratories, sexes and populations, so always use the range printed on the report. As a rough guide, adult haemoglobin is about 130 to 180 g/L in men and 115 to 165 g/L in women, mean cell volume (MCV) about 80 to 100 fL, white cell count about 4 to 11 x 10^9/L and platelets about 150 to 400 x 10^9/L. Anaemia is classified by MCV into microcytic, normocytic and macrocytic, which narrows the causes before further tests.

blocks.caption: Hct is haematocrit (fraction of blood volume occupied by red cells), RBC is the red cell count, MCH is mean cell haemoglobin and Retic_abs is the absolute reticulocyte count (10^9/L when RBC is in 10^12/L and the percentage is converted to a fraction).

rows: Iron deficiency, thalassaemia trait, anaemia of chronic disease
Ferritin, iron studies, haemoglobin electrophoresis, look for blood loss
Acute blood loss, anaemia of chronic disease, chronic kidney disease, early haemolysis or marrow failure
Reticulocyte count, creatinine, film, haemolysis screen
Vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, alcohol, hypothyroidism, liver disease, some drugs, myelodysplasia
B12 and folate, thyroid and liver tests, film
blocks.caption: Classifying anaemia by mean cell volume.

blocks.title: Calculating red cell indices
blocks.prompt: A woman has Hb 92 g/L, RBC 4.4 x 10^12/L, haematocrit 0.31 L/L and a reticulocyte percentage of 0.9%. Calculate MCV, MCH and the absolute reticulocyte count, and interpret them.

steps.text: Calculate MCV. MCV = Hct / RBC x 1000 = 0.31 / 4.4 x 1000 = 70.5 fL, which is below the typical lower limit of about 80 fL, so the cells are microcytic.
Calculate MCH. MCH = Hb / RBC = 92 / 4.4 = 20.9 pg, below the typical range, so the cells are also low in haemoglobin (hypochromic).
Calculate the absolute reticulocyte count. 0.9% of 4.4 x 10^12/L is 0.009 x 4400 x 10^9/L = 39.6 x 10^9/L. This is not raised, so the marrow is not responding as expected to the anaemia.

Interpret. Microcytic, hypochromic anaemia with an inadequate reticulocyte response fits impaired haemoglobin synthesis, most commonly iron deficiency. A ferritin and a search for blood loss are the next steps, particularly in a woman of this age.

blocks.answer: MCV 70.5 fL, MCH 20.9 pg, absolute reticulocyte count about 40 x 10^9/L: microcytic hypochromic anaemia with poor marrow response, most likely iron deficiency until proven otherwise.

blocks.markdown: **The blood film and coagulation screen.** The film shows what the counter cannot. Hypochromic microcytes with pencil cells suggest iron deficiency; hypersegmented neutrophils with oval macrocytes suggest B12 or folate deficiency; spherocytes suggest hereditary spherocytosis or autoimmune haemolysis; fragmented red cells (schistocytes) suggest mechanical destruction as in microangiopathic haemolysis; sickle cells and target cells point to haemoglobinopathies; circulating blasts suggest acute leukaemia. For coagulation, the prothrombin time (reported as the INR) reflects the extrinsic and common pathways and is prolonged by warfarin, vitamin K deficiency and liver disease; the activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT) reflects the intrinsic and common pathways and is prolonged by unfractionated heparin and by haemophilia; in disseminated intravascular coagulation, platelets and fibrinogen fall, and D-dimer rises.

rows: Loss of membrane, cells less deformable
Microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, disseminated intravascular coagulation
blocks.caption: Key blood film abnormalities.

blocks.markdown: **Blood groups and compatibility.** Red cells carry A and/or B antigens (ABO system) and, on a separate system, the RhD antigen. People naturally make antibodies against the ABO antigens they lack, which is why a mismatched transfusion can cause rapid intravascular haemolysis. Group O red cells have neither A nor B antigen so are the universal red cell donor type; group AB plasma has neither anti-A nor anti-B so is the universal plasma donor type. RhD-negative recipients, especially girls and women of child-bearing potential, should receive RhD-negative red cells to prevent anti-D formation. Before transfusion the laboratory performs a group and antibody screen and, depending on local policy, a crossmatch or electronic issue.

blocks.caption: ABO compatibility for red cells and plasma.

blocks.title: Choosing compatible components in haemorrhage
blocks.prompt: A 28-year-old woman, group A RhD-negative on a recent sample, is bleeding heavily after childbirth. Which red cells and plasma are compatible, and what is the emergency option if her group were unknown?

steps.text: List her antibodies. Group A means she has anti-B antibodies, so she must not receive red cells carrying B antigen.
Choose red cells. Compatible ABO groups are A and O; as she is a woman of child-bearing potential and RhD-negative, the red cells should also be RhD-negative (A D-negative or O D-negative).
Choose plasma. Plasma must not contain anti-A, which would attack her cells, so group A or AB plasma is compatible.

If her group were unknown. Emergency issue uses group O RhD-negative red cells (and AB plasma if needed) per the hospital major haemorrhage protocol, and a sample is sent so group-specific components can follow.

blocks.answer: Red cells A or O, RhD-negative; plasma A or AB; in a true emergency with unknown group, O RhD-negative red cells are used.

blocks.markdown: **Preventing transfusion errors.** The most serious avoidable hazard is giving the wrong blood to the wrong patient. UK haemovigilance (the Serious Hazards of Transfusion scheme) repeatedly shows that errors arise mainly from patient identification failures: wrong blood in tube at sampling, collecting the wrong unit, and skipped bedside checks. Control points are: justify and prescribe the transfusion (many guidelines use a restrictive trigger around 70 g/L in non-bleeding patients, but follow current guidance); take the pre-transfusion sample with full patient identity checked at the bedside and labelled there; collect the right unit with a second check; perform the final bedside check of patient identity band against the unit label by a trained staff member; and observe the patient (typically temperature, pulse, blood pressure and respiratory rate before starting, shortly after starting and at the end). Any mismatch means the unit is not given.

rows: Fever, rigors, loin or chest pain, hypotension, red urine, bleeding from lines
Stop transfusion, check identity, resuscitate, call senior help, send samples and unit to the laboratory
Temperature rise with chills, otherwise stable
Stop or slow and review; exclude haemolysis and sepsis before continuing
Pause, assess, treat symptoms and review before restarting
Stop transfusion and follow the anaphylaxis algorithm, including intramuscular adrenaline
Breathlessness, hypertension, raised jugular venous pressure, crackles, usually elderly or cardiac patient
Stop, sit upright, oxygen and diuretic per medical review
Acute hypoxia and bilateral pulmonary infiltrates within about 6 hours, often hypotension or fever, no overload
Stop, supportive respiratory care, report to the blood service
High fever, rigors, hypotension, often with platelets
Stop, cultures of patient and unit, broad-spectrum antibiotics
blocks.caption: Recognition and first response to common transfusion reactions.

blocks.title: A temperature rise during transfusion
blocks.prompt: Fifteen minutes into a unit of red cells, a 60-year-old man's temperature has risen from 36.8 degrees Celsius at baseline to 38.1 degrees Celsius. He feels slightly chilled but his pulse, blood pressure and oxygen saturation are unchanged and he has no pain, rash or breathlessness. What do you do?

steps.text: Stop or pause the transfusion and keep the intravenous line. Any new fever during a transfusion must be treated as a possible reaction until proven otherwise.
Check identity. Compare the patient's wristband, the unit label and the prescription again. A mismatch would mean an incorrect unit and an acute haemolytic reaction, which is an emergency.

Assess severity. Airway, breathing, circulation and observations are stable and there are no signs of haemolysis (no loin pain, hypotension or red urine) or anaphylaxis, so a febrile non-haemolytic reaction is likely.

Escalate and decide. A doctor reviews. Because fever can also signal early haemolysis or bacterial contamination, the unit and samples may be sent to the laboratory, and restarting depends on review and local policy. The event is documented and reported to the hospital transfusion team.

blocks.answer: Stop, check identity, assess; a stable fever is most likely febrile non-haemolytic but only after haemolysis and sepsis are considered, with senior review and reporting.

blocks.title: Fever, pain or hypotension in a transfusion means stop
blocks.text: Stop the transfusion first, then think. Do not flush the giving set into the patient, keep the line open with a fresh saline set, recheck identity and call for senior help. The most dangerous reaction, ABO-incompatible haemolysis, is almost always caused by an identification error at the bedside or at sampling.

points: Read the FBC by line, classify anaemia by MCV, and confirm with the film, reticulocyte count and targeted tests; reference ranges vary by laboratory.
Calculate MCV from haematocrit and red cell count, MCH from haemoglobin and red cell count, and the absolute reticulocyte count from the percentage and red cell count.
Group O red cells and group AB plasma are the universal donor types; RhD-negative recipients, particularly women of child-bearing potential, receive RhD-negative red cells.
Most serious errors are patient identification failures; use positive identification at sampling and a final bedside check.
Stop the transfusion in any suspected reaction, recheck identity and assess airway, breathing and circulation; TACO has overload features whereas TRALI shows acute lung injury without them.

questions.stem: A 62-year-old man has Hb 78 g/L, MCV 68 fL and a low ferritin. The blood film shows hypochromic microcytes with pencil cells. What is the best interpretation and next step?

options.text: Vitamin B12 deficiency; start folate alone
Anaemia of acute haemorrhage; no further tests needed
Iron deficiency anaemia; look for a source of blood loss, particularly in the gastrointestinal tract
Haemolytic anaemia; plan splenectomy

questions.correctOptionText: Iron deficiency anaemia; look for a source of blood loss, particularly in the gastrointestinal tract

distractorRationale.a: B12 deficiency causes macrocytosis with hypersegmented neutrophils, and folate alone can be harmful when B12 is low.
distractorRationale.b: Acute bleeding is usually normocytic, and this picture suggests a chronic process needing a cause.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: microcytosis, hypochromia, pencil cells and low ferritin indicate iron deficiency, and in a man of this age the cause is until proven otherwise occult blood loss.
distractorRationale.d: Haemolysis causes spherocytes or fragments and raised reticulocytes, not hypochromic microcytes with low ferritin.

questions.explanation: A low ferritin with a microcytic hypochromic film is diagnostic of iron deficiency in practice, and the key clinical step is to find the cause. In an older man this usually means investigating the gastrointestinal tract for blood loss rather than just giving iron.

questions.stem: A 33-year-old woman has fever, confusion, Hb 70 g/L and platelets 18 x 10^9/L. The film shows many fragmented red cells (schistocytes) and the lactate dehydrogenase is raised. What does the film indicate?

options.text: Mechanical destruction of red cells in small vessels (microangiopathic haemolysis), needing urgent specialist assessment
Iron deficiency
Vitamin B12 deficiency
Hereditary spherocytosis

questions.correctOptionText: Mechanical destruction of red cells in small vessels (microangiopathic haemolysis), needing urgent specialist assessment

distractorRationale.a: Correct: schistocytes with thrombocytopenia and raised LDH indicate microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia, a haematological emergency.
distractorRationale.b: Iron deficiency shows hypochromic microcytes, not fragments, and does not cause fragmentation.
distractorRationale.c: B12 deficiency shows macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils.
distractorRationale.d: Hereditary spherocytosis shows spherocytes and is not associated with fragmentation and acute illness.

questions.explanation: Fragmented red cells are the film hallmark of mechanical shearing in small vessels, which together with a low platelet count and neurological or renal features signals a thrombotic microangiopathy needing urgent same-day haematology input. The other conditions each have different film appearances.

questions.stem: A patient is blood group B RhD-positive. Which red cell groups are ABO compatible for transfusion?

options.text: Group A and group AB
Group A and group B
Group AB only
Group B and group O

distractorRationale.a: Group A cells carry the A antigen that the patient's anti-A would attack.
distractorRationale.b: Group A cells would be attacked, so this pair is incompatible.
distractorRationale.c: Group AB cells carry A antigen so they would be attacked.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: the patient has anti-A antibodies, so red cells must lack the A antigen, which means B or O.

questions.explanation: A group B patient has anti-A in plasma, so red cells with A antigen cause haemolysis. Only B or O red cells lack A antigen and are ABO compatible.

questions.stem: Which single step most directly addresses the commonest cause of ABO-incompatible transfusion, wrong blood in tube?

options.text: Giving all patients group O red cells
Positive identification of the patient at the bedside when the sample is taken, with labelling at the bedside
Transfusing only during daytime hours
Checking the unit label against the prescription only after completion

questions.correctOptionText: Positive identification of the patient at the bedside when the sample is taken, with labelling at the bedside

distractorRationale.a: Group O for all would waste a scarce resource and does not address plasma or identification errors; it is not standard practice.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: the sample must be from the right patient and labelled in front of the patient, so the group result is trustworthy.
distractorRationale.c: Time of day does not remove identification errors.
distractorRationale.d: Checks must occur before the unit is connected, not afterwards.

questions.explanation: If the sample is taken from the wrong patient or mislabelled, the laboratory issues blood for the wrong group, so positive patient identification at sampling is the key control. Later bedside checks add a second safeguard, which is why both exist.

questions.stem: Ten minutes after starting a red cell unit, a woman develops rigors, severe loin pain, flushing and a fall in blood pressure; urine is dark red. What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Slow the infusion rate and reassess in one hour
Continue the unit and give an antihistamine
Stop the transfusion, keep intravenous access, recheck patient and unit identity and resuscitate
Switch to a different bag of the same unit and carry on

questions.correctOptionText: Stop the transfusion, keep intravenous access, recheck patient and unit identity and resuscitate

distractorRationale.a: Slowing still delivers incompatible cells and delays resuscitation.
distractorRationale.b: An antihistamine treats mild allergy, not haemolysis.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: this is acute haemolysis until proven otherwise, and ongoing transfusion adds antigen load.
distractorRationale.d: The product is the same, so the problem continues.

questions.explanation: The picture of rigors, loin pain, hypotension and haemoglobinuria points to acute haemolysis from an incompatible unit. Stopping the transfusion, protecting circulation and checking identity are first, followed by senior help, laboratory investigation and reporting.

questions.stem: A patient has a haematocrit of 0.34 L/L and a red cell count of 3.2 x 10^12/L. Calculate the MCV in fL.
questions.explanation: MCV = haematocrit / red cell count x 1000 = 0.34 / 3.2 x 1000 = 106.25 fL, which is above the typical upper limit of about 100 fL (ranges vary by laboratory). A macrocytic anaemia prompts B12, folate, thyroid and liver tests and a blood film.

questions.stem: A patient with anaemia has a red cell count of 2.5 x 10^12/L and 4.0% of the red cells are reticulocytes. Calculate the absolute reticulocyte count in x 10^9/L.
questions.explanation: Absolute reticulocyte count = percentage x red cell count = 0.040 x 2.5 x 10^12/L = 0.1 x 10^12/L, which is 100 x 10^9/L. A count at or above this level in an anaemic patient suggests an active marrow response, so haemolysis or recent bleeding becomes more likely than marrow failure.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old group O RhD-negative woman needs red cells for postpartum bleeding. Explain what makes red cell and plasma components compatible and describe the sequence of checks that prevent transfusing the wrong blood.
markingGuide: ABO antigens on red cells and naturally occurring antibodies in plasma
Group O red cells lack A and B antigens; plasma must not contain antibodies against recipient antigens
RhD-negative red cells for a woman of child-bearing potential
Positive patient identification and correct labelling at sampling
Laboratory group and screen, crossmatch or electronic issue
Collection of the correct unit with a check
Final bedside check of patient wristband against unit label and prescription
Observations and reporting of any mismatch or near miss
questions.explanation: Compatibility depends on matching donor antigens to the recipient's antibodies and RhD status. Safety depends on repeated identity checks, because most severe errors arise from patient identification failures.

questions.stem: Compare transfusion-associated circulatory overload with transfusion-related acute lung injury in terms of presentation, mechanism and initial management.
markingGuide: TACO: volume overload, hypertension, raised JVP, response to diuretic, at-risk elderly or cardiac patients
TRALI: non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema, bilateral infiltrates, hypoxia within about 6 hours, often hypotension or fever
Mechanism of TRALI: donor antibodies or mediators activate recipient neutrophils
Stop transfusion in both and give oxygen
TACO: sit upright and consider diuretic; TRALI: supportive respiratory care, diuretics not helpful
Report both to the hospital transfusion team and blood service
questions.explanation: Both cause respiratory distress during or after transfusion but differ in haemodynamics: overload raises pressures, while lung injury is a capillary leak with normal or low pressures. Distinguishing them guides treatment, notably the use of diuretics.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man has Hb 82 g/L, MCV 112 fL, white cell count 2.8 x 10^9/L and platelets 96 x 10^9/L. The film shows macro-ovalocytes and hypersegmented neutrophils. Outline your interpretation and initial investigations.
markingGuide: Pancytopenia with macrocytosis
Megaloblastic picture suggests vitamin B12 or folate deficiency
Other causes: myelodysplasia, alcohol, drugs, liver disease, hypothyroidism
Check B12, folate, reticulocytes, liver and thyroid tests, haematology review
Consider marrow examination if the cause is unclear or the film shows other abnormalities
Avoid giving folate alone before B12 status is known
questions.explanation: A macrocytic pancytopenia with hypersegmented neutrophils points to impaired DNA synthesis, most commonly B12 or folate deficiency, but marrow failure must be excluded. Structured tests identify the cause and prevent harm from treating the wrong deficiency.
